title: Consumer Product Safety Commission staff guidance to pharmacists on conventional-packaging requests, container reuse and institutional dispensing
subtopic: Poison prevention packaging of prescription drugs: CPSC guidance
rule_summary: The Consumer Product Safety Commission publication Poison Prevention Packaging: A Guide for Healthcare Professionals (CPSC 384, revised 2005) states the staff's views in question-and-answer form. It states that the law does not preclude a pharmacist from relying upon a specific request from a patient to have all of his or her medications placed in non-special packaging, which many pharmacies choose to have in writing as a blanket waiver; that a single request to dispense a specific prescription in non-special packaging is not a basis to infer the patient wants all subsequent prescriptions so dispensed; that the law and regulations do not require a written request, although the staff recommends getting the request in writing, particularly for a blanket waiver; and that it is a prudent practice to periodically check with patients who have blanket waiver requests on file. It states that a pharmacist may follow a physician's standing order for noncomplying packaging only for refills of the prescription for which the physician prescribed it, and that a drug dispensed on a different prescription of the same or another prescriber must be in special packaging unless that prescription directs noncomplying packaging or the purchaser requests it; that determining at the retail level whether a prescription drug must be packaged in accordance with the standards is the responsibility of the dispensing pharmacist; that, as a general rule, prescription bottles and vials may not be reused for refills, although the staff has indicated it would have no objection to reuse of a glass container provided a new closure is used; that any package containing a regulated substance, including unit dose packaging such as blisters or pouches, must meet the special packaging standards; that a tamper-evident package is not necessarily child-resistant; that drugs dispensed for patients confined in a hospital, or supplied to a traditional nursing home where staff administer doses, need not be in special packaging, unlike senior apartments or assisted living facilities where residents store their drugs in their households, the test being whether the package is likely to enter a home; and that the Commission does not approve or certify special packaging.
exam_relevance: Tests how the dispensing pharmacist applies the statute in practice as CPSC staff guidance describes it: blanket patient requests, prescriber standing orders limited to refills of that prescription, no reuse of plastic vials, unit-dose packages held to the same standard, and the institutional-use test.

authority.name: Poison Prevention Packaging: A Guide for Healthcare Professionals (CPSC 384, revised 2005)
authority.section: Questions and answers for pharmacists and physicians

common_confusions: Treating the staff's recommendation to obtain requests in writing as a legal requirement.
Treating one patient request for one prescription as a blanket waiver.
Presenting the glass-container view as a regulation rather than as staff guidance.
verification_notes: CPSC 384 (revised 2005) read in the PDF linked from the Commission's page Poison Prevention Packaging: A Guide for Healthcare Professionals during the authoring session of 2026-09-16 to 2026-09-17; the text is Commission staff guidance, not a regulation.
